text: Every chapter so far has used the AWS console — clicking through screens to launch instances and create buckets. The AWS CLI turns those same actions into commands you can type, save in a script, and run again identically a hundred times, which is what makes real automation possible. Before you can run a single command against your account, the CLI needs to know who you are and which account to talk to — that's what aws configure sets up.

Run aws configure and it asks four questions in order: your AWS access key ID, your secret access key, a default region like us-east-1, and a default output format such as json. The access key ID and secret access key come from an IAM user you created earlier in this course — never from the root account — and together they're the credential pair the CLI uses to sign every request it sends.

Those answers don't vanish into some hidden settings store — aws configure just writes two plain-text files. ~/.aws/credentials holds the access key ID and secret access key under a [default] section. ~/.aws/config holds the region and output format, also under [default]. Open either file in a text editor and you'll see exactly what's stored.

Most administrators work with more than one AWS account — a dev account, a production account, maybe a client's. Named profiles handle that: aws configure --profile prod creates a second, independent set of credentials without touching default. Here's the detail worth memorizing: in ~/.aws/credentials, that profile's section is just named [prod], but in ~/.aws/config, it's [profile prod] — every non-default profile in the config file gets a literal "profile" prefix. Any command then takes --profile to pick which account it runs against, like aws s3 ls --profile prod.

Once credentials and profiles are configured, you're ready to run real commands against real AWS resources instead of just signing in. Lesson 18 covers the aws service command pattern every CLI call follows, plus --output and --query for shaping what comes back from a busy account.
